newsitem.title: UK: Opponents hound British government on crime plans.
newsitem.headline: Opponents hound British government on crime plans.

text.p: A debate in Britain over how to create a more moral, less crime-ridden society threatened on Friday to rebound on the ruling Conservatives.
Public opinion and the opposition parties have already forced Prime Minister John Major into embarrassing U-turns in the law-and-order area, usually one of his party's strong suits.
Now he is under pressure to make further concessions to his critics, ranging from establishment figures to the normally Conservative-supporting Sun tabloid newspaper.
"The Government has failed on law and order...There is an urgent need to secure public safety," opposition Labour party home affairs spokesman Jack Straw told BBC radio on Friday.
Scotland's Dunblane tragedy, in which 16 children and a teacher were shot dead by a crazed loner, is a focal point of the morality debate which has dominated newspapers this week.
Another is the knifing to death of a London headmaster whose widow, Frances Lawrence, took a page of the Times to stress that children must be taught the difference between right and wrong.

An inquiry into Dunblane by a senior Scottish judge recommended handguns be kept in secure gun clubs. Major had promised to implement the inquiry's findings, but pressure of public opinion has forced him to go further.
The government now proposes to ban all handguns except .22 calibre target shooting weapons. But the Sun, and the opposition Labour and Liberal Democrat parties demand a complete ban.
"There is still plenty of time for another U-turn," the Sun mocked in an editorial on Friday.

It was referring to Major's sudden decision on Wednesday to allow two law-and-order measures -- one setting up a paedophile register, the other outlawing "stalking", or obsessive tracking of individuals -- to proceed in parliament as government bills.
Hours previously, the government published its legislative programme for the last session of parliament before a general election expected by May omitting the two measures.
Ministers said they should be introduced as private members' bills, although these often fail due to lack of debating time.
Labour and the Liberal Democrats hailed Major's about-face as a victory for pressure they had put on him, and on Thursday called for a further bill to outlaw so-called combat knives.
But Major spurned offers by Tony Blair and Paddy Ashdown, the leaders of the two opposition parties, of cooperation in pushing such a bill speedily through parliament.

An aide said on Friday ministers had found it impossible to frame legislation because of problems in defining a combat knife in legal terms. "Regrettably, a suitable definition which would stand in legislation has not been arrived at," he said.

Meanwhile, the government's main law-and-order bill for the new parliamentary session, to establish minimum sentences for certain crimes, ran into criticism from a former top judge who said politicians should not interfere in sentencing.
"The whole principle of justice as we know it in this country is that judges are charged with the duty of ensuring that...the criminal gets his just desserts," Lord John Donaldson told BBC radio.

But the bill was backed by Brian Mackenzie, president of the Police Superintendents' Association, who said in a statement: "These measures will sound a powerful message that society is now prepared to fight back (against criminals)."

Major believes Blair will be unable to accept the sentencing plans, which will prove popular with ordinary Britons, helping the prime minister to claw back a 14-20 point Labour lead in the opinion polls.
Heir to the throne Prince Charles joined in the debate on Friday when he called for a scheme under which 25,000 young people a year would volunteer for work to improve their communities.
